title: Distinct Pairs a Fixed Gap Apart
statement:
You get an integer array nums and an integer k ≥ 0. Count the distinct value pairs (x, y) with x ≤ y and y − x == k, where x and y come from two different positions of nums.

Pairs are counted by value: however many copies of x and y there are, the pair (x, y) counts once.

examples.why: (1, 3), (3, 5), (5, 7) and (7, 9). The second 5 does not create extra pairs.
With k = 0 a value must appear at least twice: only (3, 3). A lone 1 cannot pair with itself.

hints: Duplicates do not create new pairs. What is the right thing to iterate over: positions or distinct values?
For k > 0, a distinct value x has a partner exactly when x + k is also present.
Count each value. For k > 0 count keys x with x + k present; for k = 0 count keys that appear at least twice.

explain.intuition:
Because pairs are counted by value, collapse the array into a frequency map. Each distinct value x can only be the smaller end of one pair: (x, x + k). So for k > 0 the answer is the number of keys x for which x + k is also a key.

k = 0 is the trap: x + 0 is x itself, which is always "present", but a pair needs two different positions. Here you count the values that occur at least twice.
steps: If k == 0, return the number of values with frequency ≥ 2.
Otherwise, return the number of keys x with x + k also a key.
pitfalls: Treating k = 0 like any other k, which counts every distinct value as a pair with itself.
Counting both (x, x + k) and (x − k, x) for each x, which doubles the answer.
Counting pairs of positions instead of distinct value pairs, so duplicates inflate the result.

solutions.title: All position pairs into a set
solutions.idea: Check every pair of positions and store qualifying value pairs in a set to drop repeats.

solutions.title: Frequency map
solutions.idea: Look up x + k for each distinct x; k = 0 means a value seen at least twice.

followups: Solve it in O(1) extra space after sorting, with two pointers.
Count pairs whose gap is at most k instead of exactly k.
